tagline.text: Manila's new riverside promenade beside Intramuros

location.label: Location
location.text: North bank of the Pasig River, Manila (Central Post Office to Fort Santiago in Intramuros to Arroceros Park)

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱0~900 (free entry; snacks, dinner and transport included)

children.text: This free riverside promenade of about 1.9 km runs from behind the Manila Central Post Office to Fort Santiago in Intramuros. It is car-free and flat, so it is easy to walk, and it fills with people especially at sunset and in the evening.

The Pasig River Esplanade is a pedestrian-only promenade built along the north bank of the Pasig River, which runs through Manila. Its official project name is "Pasig: Bigyang Buhay Muli" (Give Life Again). It is part of the Marcos administration's Pasig River rehabilitation effort and is known as a project of special interest to First Lady Liza Araneta-Marcos. The master plan was prepared by WTA Architecture and Design Studio and PGAA Creative Design.
The plan calls for a riverside promenade of about
25 km
across Manila, Mandaluyong, Makati, Pasig and Taguig. The part you can walk today is the first section: as of April 2026 the four completed phases total about
, though some sources round this to "about 2 km." It starts at Fort Santiago (Intramuros) and continues past the back of the Central Post Office, Jones Bridge, Plaza Mexico and Arroceros Forest Park.
The phases opened as follows. Phase 1A,
from the Central Post Office to Jones Bridge, opened on January 17, 2024. The
from Jones Bridge to Plaza Mexico opened on June 23, 2024, and the
from Plaza Mexico to Fort Santiago opened on February 27, 2025. Phase 4,
from the Central Post Office to Arroceros Park, opened in October 2025. Opening dates differ by about a day depending on the outlet.

For travelers, it pairs well with sightseeing in Intramuros. By day you walk past old buildings and the river, and after dark lighting and street food change the mood. Entry is free and the path is flat, so it is easy with children or parents. Some stretches have little shade, so bring a hat and water during the day. It is considered suitable for families, couples and first-time visitors in central Metro Manila. If you expect nature or water activities you may be disappointed, so think of it as an urban stroll. As you walk you will also notice old buildings such as the Aduana (Customs) building and the Bureau of Immigration, and the ruins of the Maestranza Wall and Puerta de Almacenes.

blocks.title: The main stretch behind the Central Post Office

children.text: Phase 1A is the esplanade's photo spot. Riverside benches and walkways run against the backdrop of the neoclassical Manila Central Post Office. There is little shade, so late afternoon is the better time. The building was begun in 1926 and completed in February 1928, designed by Juan Arellano, Tomás Mapúa and Ralph Doane. It is known for its 16 Ionic columns at the entrance and was declared an important cultural property by the National Museum in 2018. A major fire on the night of May 21, 2023 burned for more than 30 hours, and restoration is under way, so the condition of the exterior may change.

blocks.title: The Maestranza Wall and Plaza Mexico

children.text: Phase 3, from Plaza Mexico to Fort Santiago, includes the Maestranza Esplanade and the
Fort Santiago Riverwalk. Trees give shade and make it pleasant to walk, and the route passes beside ruins of the Spanish-era wall.
Phase 1C has stalls, shops and a food bazaar where you can enjoy street food from dusk until midnight. Snacks are said to cost about
each and milk tea about
Crossing Jones Bridge leads straight to Escolta Street and Binondo. The esplanade and an old-town tour combine well into a one-day itinerary.
The end of Phase 4 meets the Arroceros urban forest park. It is relatively cool thanks to the trees, and the Metropolitan Theater, Manila City Hall and LRT-1 Central Station are close by.

blocks.title: Linking up with the Pasig River Ferry

children.text: The Escolta, Lawton and Quinta ferry stations are within walking distance. You can also ride the ferry in, walk the esplanade, and return by ferry.

blocks.title: A route for wheelchairs and strollers

children.text: The path is flat and has ramps instead of steps, so wheelchairs, walkers and strollers are said to move easily. Because cars cannot enter, it is safe to walk.
In the evening the riverside lights come on and the mood changes. Private night river cruises are also described, starting from about
per person. Prices and operations can change, so confirm before booking.
Start from LRT-1 Central Terminal Station or the Lawton area and walk toward Arroceros Park on Phase 4.
Take photos and rest on a bench at Phase 1A behind the Central Post Office.
Walk toward Plaza Mexico and look at the ruins of the Maestranza Wall and the river views.
Walk toward Fort Santiago along Phase 3 and enjoy the evening light. Entering Fort Santiago requires a separate fee.
Return to the Phase 1C food bazaar for dinner. The bazaar is known to operate from 18:00 until midnight.
Shops and stalls are said to open from about 15:00 until midnight. In the dry season, the golden sunset between 17:00 and 18:30 is the prettiest.

items.title: Ferry combo course
items.subtitle: Arrive by river and walk the riverside

children.text: Board the Pasig River Ferry at an upstream station such as Guadalupe. A valid ID is required.
Get off at Escolta Station and walk toward Jones Bridge.
Have lunch in Binondo or Escolta.
Walk the esplanade and see Intramuros, then return via Lawton Station or the LRT.
From Ninoy Aquino International Airport (NAIA), take a ride-hailing taxi such as Grab to the Central Post Office or Intramuros. Depending on traffic it can take
40 minutes–1 hour 30 minutes
or more.
Set your destination as "Manila Central Post Office (Magallanes Drive)."
Getting off at LRT-1 Central Terminal Station connects you directly to Phase 4.
From LRT-1 Carriedo Station, take a jeepney toward Plaza Roma and walk to Plaza Mexico.
Several bus routes pass around Manila City Hall, and app-based taxis such as Grab and Move It are also available.

The Escolta, Lawton and Quinta stations are close to the promenade. Escolta Station is next to Plaza Yuchengco behind the Bureau of Immigration, Lawton Station is near Quezon Bridge and the Central Post Office, and Quinta Station is behind Quinta Market near Quiapo Church.

2026 information also says it is free and you only need to show an ID. It runs during the day: hours vary by station, starting around 7 a.m. with the last boat leaving between about 5 and 6 p.m. (18:30 in some guides). Many guides say it runs Monday to Saturday, with no service on Sundays or at night.
Seats are first come, first served with no reservations, and service can be cut short by events or weather, so check the latest MMDA announcements.
Travelers report that Guadalupe to Escolta takes about
50–60 minutes
excluding waiting time. Several trips run daily; check the exact timetable at the station.
Parking is first-come street parking near the Maestranza area, on Magallanes Drive, and behind and beside the Central Post Office.
You can also park in Intramuros and walk through Fort Santiago, and on the Binondo side you can use the Escolta car park.
Parking is very limited, so public transport or ride-hailing is far easier.
The dry season, November to April, is best. During the day it is busiest and most atmospheric from around 5 p.m. until 9 p.m., as the sun lowers. Tuesday to Thursday is said to be relatively quiet.
There is little shade on Phases 1A and 1C, so it is hot by day. In the rainy season showers come suddenly and winds are strong, so some guides recommend a raincoat rather than an umbrella.
The golden hour in the dry season is described as roughly 17:00–18:30. Evenings from November to April on weekdays have the best atmosphere; in the rainy season, bring a raincoat.

rows: The best time for a stroll; the evening hours are popular

The area is close to Intramuros and the hotel districts of Ermita and Malate. There is no lodging on the promenade itself, so most visitors stay in Intramuros, Ermita, Malate or the Manila Bay area and walk or take a taxi.

Food centers on the street food at the Phase 1C food bazaar. You can enjoy skewers, sisig, desserts and milk tea. For a proper meal, cross Jones Bridge to a Chinese restaurant in Binondo or a café on the Escolta side. It is not certain where ATMs are, so it is best to have small bills ready. A Dubai chocolate dessert is described at about ₱300 and pork sisig at about ₱199, but prices differ by stall, so treat these only as a guide. An evening for a couple including the ferry and dinner is estimated at roughly ₱600~900.
Arrive around 5 p.m., watch the sunset and stay for the lit night scenery for the most satisfying visit.
Some sections have little shade, so bring a hat, sunscreen and water during the day.
Tuesday to Thursday is relatively quiet. Weekend evenings can be very crowded.
Pedestrians have priority on the promenade. Walk your bicycle on narrow paths.
Shops and the food bazaar open around sunset, so there may be little to eat during the day.
Public restrooms are paid, so bring small change.
Bring ID if you ride the ferry, and check the latest timetable on MMDA announcements.
Combine it with Fort Santiago and Intramuros for a natural one-day itinerary.
In crowded hours, watch out for pickpockets and phone snatchers; drones, pets and littering are said to be prohibited.
Swimming is not possible from the promenade and kayaking is described as impractical. Stay away from the water.
A fine of ₱500 for littering is reported. Rules may change.
Midday in summer is very hot with little shade. Beware of heatstroke.
Do not go alone into remote stretches late at night. Stay in busy sections for safety.
Open sections and operating hours are still being expanded and adjusted, so check for the latest news.
A Spanish-era fortress reached through a side gate at the end of Phase 3. It is famous as the place where José Rizal was imprisoned.
An old commercial street reached by crossing Jones Bridge, with cafés and Art Deco buildings.
Called the oldest Chinatown in the world, it is famous for Chinese food and street food.
An Art Deco theater near Arroceros Park, worth a stop to see its exterior.
The walled city that connects to Fort Santiago at the end of the promenade, making a full-day itinerary.
